Fortunately, the investment grade side of the AI credit ecosystem remains well-behaved given the strong fundamentals of the hyperscalers (or at least most of them), so the glass-half-full interpretation is that the unraveling in the high yield AI names could actually be a good thing in that it might bring some discipline to the compute buildout and slow it down. In the process, that could help make this capex boom more sustainable and avoid a repeat of the overbuilt internet bubble of the late 1990’s. 🧵(3/3)

However, parts of the credit market are telling a different story, so perhaps the bubble (if there is one) is not on the equity valuation side but on the debt side. Many of us remember the https://t.co/IHUthcKRRV silly season of the internet bubble, but the early warnings came from the debt side, namely telecom. If the fiber optics over-buildout during the 1990s is akin to the datacenter buildout today, then there is a lesson to be learned from the credit markets. Below I show the yield on the Bloomberg high yield telecom index back then against the yield on CRWV bonds today. Makes you wonder. 🧵(2/3)

BREAKING: The NAHB Housing Market Index fell -3 points in October, to 29, its lowest level since June 2012.

This marks the 2nd consecutive monthly decline in homebuilder sentiment, totaling -6 points, marking the largest 2-month decrease since June 2025.

All 3 components deteriorated, with current sales falling -2 points, to 33, the lowest since June 2012.

Sales expectations dropped -5 points, to 32, the lowest since November 2022, while buyer traffic plunged -5 points, to 18, the lowest since April 2012, excluding the 2020 pandemic.

Furthermore, 43% of builders cut prices this month, the highest proportion of any month from 2020 to 2026.

The affordability crisis is putting further pressure on homebuilder sentiment.

US private equity firms are struggling to attract new capital:

Private equity funds raised just $222 billion from investors in the first 9 months of 2026, on track for the weakest year since 2020. 

This would also mark the 3rd consecutive annual decline.

By comparison, the industry attracted $406 billion in full year 2023 and $330 billion last year.

Higher rates have made it harder for private equity firms to sell businesses at attractive prices, weakening investment returns and prompting investors to become more reluctant to commit capital to new funds.

Smaller firms managing less than $15 billion are facing the most pressure.

Private equity has lost its shine in the rapidly evolving macroeconomic backdrop.

If this trend persists, rates could stay higher for longer. Indeed, that has been the narrative recently, until late last week. Note below that while the 50-day correlation continues to be negative between crude oil and the S&P 500, and positive between crude oil and bond prices, the correlation between bonds and the relative performance of the GS AI basket vs the ex-AI basket has now flipped negative. In other words, AI appears to have become systemic enough that its underperformance is causing yields to fall. 🧵(3/3)

But on the other side of that spectrum is the Middle East, and with apparently no end insight to the conflict, crude oil prices are back above $100. More importantly, the Brent 9th forward contract keeps making steady new highs and is $7 higher than it was in February. When the conflict started and the oil strip was in deep backwardation, there seemed to be a consensus that the forwards were correct (by being lower) and that the front contract was temporarily dislocated (too high). It turns out that it was the other way around. 🧵(2/3)

The action late last week was fascinating in that the sell-off in AI names led to a move lower in bond yields. Perhaps it’s just a risk-off impulse that will soon dissipate, but perhaps the AI boom has gotten so big that it has become systemic to the economy and therefore monetary policy and inflation. 🧵(1/3)

BREAKING: Foreign holdings of US Treasuries jumped +$83 billion in August, to $9.33 trillion, their 6th-highest total on record.

The surge was driven by Canada, which raised its holdings by +$38 billion, to $465 billion, its 4th-highest on record.

This was followed by Belgium, which increased its holdings by +$20 billion, to a record $491 billion.

The UK, the 2nd-largest holder, raised its holdings by +$11 billion, to a record $1.01 trillion.

Meanwhile, Japan, the largest foreign holder, cut its holdings by -$36 billion, to $1.07 trillion, its lowest since November 2024.

China, the 3rd-largest holder, reduced its holdings by -$27 billion, to $591 billion, its lowest level since August 2008.

Foreign holdings of US Treasuries are rising despite continued selling in Japan and China.

BREAKING: US housing starts fell -5.2% MoM in September, to an annualized rate of 1.22 million, the 2nd-lowest reading since May 2020.

This follows MoM declines of -4.9% and -5.9% in July and August.

Single-family housing starts dropped -4.6% MoM last month, to 859,000, the 2nd-lowest since April 2023.

At the same time, multifamily housing starts fell -7.2%, to 349,000, the 2nd-lowest since May 2025.

Higher mortgage rates and worsening affordability are heavily weighing on housing demand.

Furthermore, elevated housing inventories and falling homebuilder confidence are discouraging new construction.

The US housing market is frozen.

AI-related borrowing is skyrocketing.

US Dollar-denominated AI-related corporate bond issuance is up to $419 billion so far in 2026, the highest annual figure on record.

This represents a +90% YoY increase from full-year 2025 and a +437% increase from full-year 2024.

Year-to-date, Alphabet, $GOOGL, Amazon, $AMZN, Meta, $META, Microsoft, $MSFT, and Oracle, $ORCL, have issued a combined $157 billion in corporate bonds, accounting for 37% of the total.

This is followed by investment-grade and high-yield data center and computing companies, which have raised $66 billion and $37 billion, respectively, and together account for ~25% of AI-related issuance.

Other AI-linked corporate bonds have represented $159 billion, or 38%.

The AI revolution is driving an unprecedented wave of corporate borrowing.
